description: Kennedy's New Frontier, Nixon and Watergate, Reagan's revolution, and the Clinton years.
content_html:
Kennedy and the New Frontier, 1961–1963

John F. Kennedy was inaugurated as the 35th President of the United States on 20 January 1961, the youngest man ever elected to the office. His domestic programme — the New Frontier — was ambitious: expanding federal aid to education, introducing Medicare to provide healthcare for the elderly, protecting civil rights and tackling poverty. However, Kennedy faced a conservative Congress that blocked much of his domestic agenda. He had more success in foreign policy, particularly in managing the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) and launching the Space Race with the Apollo programme.

Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas, Texas, on 22 November 1963. His vice president, Lyndon B. Johnson, used Kennedy’s memory and his own political skill to pass landmark legislation that Kennedy had been unable to get through Congress, including the Civil Rights Act (1964) and his “Great Society” programme of welfare expansion.

Key Fact

Kennedy’s New Frontier aimed to tackle poverty, extend civil rights, expand education and create Medicare. Much was blocked by Congress during his lifetime. After his assassination (22 November 1963), Johnson’s Great Society actually delivered many of these goals, including Medicare (1965) and the Civil Rights Act (1964).

Nixon and Watergate, 1972–1974

Richard Nixon won the 1968 and 1972 presidential elections by large margins. He achieved significant foreign policy successes — opening diplomatic relations with China in 1972 and negotiating the SALT I arms limitation treaty with the USSR. However, his presidency was destroyed by the Watergate scandal. On 17 June 1972, operatives working for Nixon’s re-election campaign broke into the Democratic Party headquarters at the Watergate Hotel in Washington D.C. to plant listening devices. Nixon was not directly involved in ordering the break-in, but he participated in covering up the White House connection.

Investigative journalists from the Washington Post and Congressional investigations gradually exposed the cover-up. White House tape recordings proved Nixon’s involvement. When the Supreme Court unanimously ruled in United States v Nixon (1974) that he must hand over the tapes, impeachment became inevitable. Nixon resigned on 9 August 1974 — the only US president to have resigned from office. Vice President Gerald Ford assumed the presidency and controversially pardoned Nixon.

Watergate had profound effects on American political life. Public trust in government collapsed: opinion polls from the late 1970s showed record levels of cynicism about political institutions. Congress passed the War Powers Act (1973) and campaign finance reform legislation to limit executive power. The suffix “-gate” entered the language to describe political scandals.

The Reagan Years, 1981–1989

Ronald Reagan won the 1980 election in a landslide, capitalising on economic stagflation and the Iran hostage crisis under President Carter. Reagan’s domestic economic programme — nicknamed Reaganomics — combined large tax cuts (particularly for high earners), deregulation of industries, reduced federal spending on social programmes and tight monetary policy. Supporters argued this “trickle-down” approach unleashed economic growth; critics argued it increased inequality and cut services for the poor.

Key Fact

Reaganomics combined tax cuts, deregulation, reduced social spending and tight monetary control. By the mid-1980s inflation had fallen sharply and economic growth resumed. However, income inequality grew and the federal deficit increased substantially as tax cuts outpaced spending reductions. Reagan also tripled the national debt during his presidency.

George H. W. Bush and Bill Clinton

Reagan’s vice president, George H. W. Bush, won the 1988 election but lost to Bill Clinton in 1992 largely because of a recession. Clinton’s campaign emphasised economic issues with the phrase “It’s the economy, stupid.” Clinton presided over a prolonged economic expansion in the 1990s, aided by the technology boom. He pursued centrist “Third Way” politics — accepting elements of both liberal and conservative approaches — and oversaw welfare reform (1996) that reduced the federal welfare rolls.

Despite his economic record, Clinton’s second term was dominated by scandal. He was impeached by the House of Representatives in December 1998 on charges of perjury and obstruction of justice related to his relationship with a White House intern. The Senate acquitted him in February 1999, and he remained in office. The episode was seen by many as a politically motivated attack by Republican opponents; others saw it as a serious matter of presidential integrity. Clinton left office in January 2001 with high approval ratings.
exam_tip_html: For 16-mark period essays on US political change 1960–2000, the examiners expect you to trace change across the whole period and reach a substantiated judgement. Don’t just describe each president in turn — identify a theme (e.g. changing public trust; the shift from liberal to conservative politics; the growing power of scandal in politics) and argue how much change occurred. Use precise evidence: Nixon resigned 9 August 1974; Reagan cut the top rate of income tax from 70% to 28%; Clinton was impeached December 1998.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Kennedy’s New Frontier (1961–63) was largely blocked by Congress, but Johnson’s Great Society delivered many of the same goals. Nixon’s Watergate scandal (1972–74) led to his resignation on 9 August 1974 — the first and only presidential resignation in US history.
  • Reagan’s economic policy (Reaganomics) combined tax cuts, deregulation and reduced social spending. It reduced inflation and stimulated growth but widened inequality and increased the national debt.
  • Clinton won in 1992 on economic issues, presided over the 1990s technology boom, but was impeached in 1998 on charges of perjury and obstruction. The Senate acquitted him and he served out his term.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Kennedy's 'New Frontier' domestic programme.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names feature (plans for Medicare; federal aid to education; civil rights legislation; tackling poverty) AND develops it. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Watergate scandal (1972-1974).
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. (1) In June 1972 operatives from Nixon's re-election campaign broke into Democratic Party headquarters at the Watergate Hotel to plant listening devices; (2) Nixon participated in covering up White House involvement and resigned on 9 August 1974 when impeachment became inevitable. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of Nixon's resignation in 1974.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies cause (the cover-up; White House tape recordings; Supreme Court ruling in United States v Nixon; Congressional investigations) AND develops the chain of reasoning explaining how it led to resignation. Secure: Cause with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Reaganomics for American society in the 1980s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies consequence (reduced inflation and economic growth; increased income inequality; growth of national debt; cuts to social programmes affecting poor Americans; deregulation of industries) AND develops the chain of effects. Secure: Consequence with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Watergate scandal for US political development.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (first presidential resignation; collapse of public trust in government; congressional investigations limiting executive power; War Powers Act 1973) AND over time (lasting decline in public trust in political institutions; 'gate' suffix for scandals; precedent for presidential accountability; contrast with Clinton's survival of impeachment). Secure: One time frame well-covered. Developing: Describes Watergate without analysing significance. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: 'The most significant political change in the USA between 1960 and 2000 was the shift from liberal to conservative politics.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Argues the case for (Kennedy/LBJ Great Society liberalism gave way to Reagan's conservatism from 1980; tax cuts replaced social spending; deregulation reversed New Deal era regulation; Clinton's Third Way accepted conservative economic framework) AGAINST (civil rights legislation under LBJ a major liberal change; Watergate showed limits of executive power; Clinton's social liberalism on healthcare and welfare). Substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Clear argument on both sides. Developing: Describes presidents without developing an argument. Emerging: Narrative.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the name of Kennedy's domestic policy programme?
On what date did President Nixon resign from office?
Reagan's economic policy, combining tax cuts and deregulation, was nicknamed '_____'.
Clinton was impeached by the House of Representatives in _____, though the Senate later acquitted him.
Match each president to a key event in their presidency:
right: Presided over the 1990s economic boom; impeached by the House in 1998
Resigned on 9 August 1974 over the Watergate cover-up
Launched the New Frontier and was assassinated in Dallas in 1963

flashcard_questions.q: What was Kennedy's domestic programme called?
When was Kennedy assassinated and where?
What happened at the Watergate Hotel on 17 June 1972?
flashcard_questions.a: Operatives from Nixon's campaign broke in to plant listening devices at Democratic Party headquarters.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Nixon resign and why?
flashcard_questions.a: 9 August 1974, facing inevitable impeachment over the Watergate cover-up.
Reagan's policy of tax cuts, deregulation, reduced social spending and tight monetary control.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the key slogan of Clinton's 1992 campaign?
When was Clinton impeached by the House of Representatives?
On what charge was Clinton impeached?
What was the outcome of Clinton's Senate trial in 1999?
flashcard_questions.a: He was acquitted and remained in office.

flashcard_questions.q: What foreign policy achievement did Nixon accomplish in 1972?
flashcard_questions.a: He opened diplomatic relations with China.

flashcard_questions.q: Which legislation did LBJ pass that Kennedy had been unable to get through Congress?
flashcard_questions.a: The Civil Rights Act (1964) and the Great Society welfare programme.

glossary_terms.definition: Kennedy's domestic policy programme, promising to tackle poverty, extend civil rights and invest in education, space exploration and healthcare.

The political scandal in which operatives of Nixon's re-election campaign broke into the Democratic Party headquarters at the Watergate Hotel in June 1972, followed by Nixon's attempts to cover up White House involvement.
Reagan's economic policy combining tax cuts (especially for high earners and corporations), deregulation, reduced social spending and tight monetary policy to control inflation.
41st President of the USA (1989-1993), who oversaw the end of the Cold War, the Gulf War of 1991 and German reunification, but lost re-election in 1992 largely due to economic recession.

items.title: Crash Course US History — Kennedy to Clinton
items.description: Crash Course's US History series covers Kennedy's New Frontier, Nixon's Watergate resignation, Reagan's conservatism and Clinton's presidency across several episodes.

items.title: Mark Felton Productions — Cold War Presidency
items.description: Mark Felton's channel covers the Cold War political context of the Kennedy, Nixon and Reagan presidencies with detailed research.

items.title: All the President's Men (1976)
items.description: Drama following Washington Post journalists Woodward and Bernstein as they investigate the Watergate break-in — essential viewing for understanding how the cover-up unravelled.

items.title: Frost/Nixon (2008)
items.description: Dramatises David Frost's 1977 television interviews with Richard Nixon, in which Nixon's admission of wrongdoing gave the American public the closest thing to a presidential confession.

items.title: JFK (1991)
items.description: Oliver Stone's film examines the assassination of President Kennedy in Dallas on 22 November 1963 and its aftermath — useful for thinking about the political impact of Kennedy's death.

items.title: Britannica — Watergate Scandal
items.description: Detailed article on the June 1972 break-in, Nixon's cover-up, the White House tape recordings, the Supreme Court's ruling in United States v Nixon and his resignation on 9 August 1974.

items.title: Britannica — Reaganomics
items.description: Encyclopaedia article explaining Reagan's economic policy of tax cuts, deregulation and reduced social spending, and the debate over whether trickle-down economics worked.

items.title: Britannica — John F. Kennedy
items.description: Biography covering Kennedy's New Frontier domestic programme, the Cuban Missile Crisis, his assassination in November 1963 and his legacy for Johnson's Great Society.

items.title: Britannica — Richard Nixon
items.description: Biography covering Nixon's foreign policy successes (China, SALT I) alongside the Watergate scandal that ended his presidency — useful for weighing his mixed legacy.

items.title: Britannica — Ronald Reagan
items.description: Biography of Reagan covering his 1980 election victory, his economic and social policies, the Iran-Contra affair, and his role in the final years of the Cold War.
